Tennis.body:
Five British tennis players have direct entry into the singles main draws at the 2026 US Open from 30 August – 13 September, with more set for qualifying. In the women’s singles, Emma Raducanu is the highest-ranked British player and will be hoping to make her return from injury.

Raducanu has been out with a stress fracture in her lower right leg, coming off the back of her first WTA 500 final at the HSBC Championships. The British No.1 has withdrawn from the National Bank Open and Cincinnati Open in the coming weeks, but will be aiming to play at the tournament she famously won in 2021.

Tennis.title: Jack Draper misses out on 2026 US Open main draw as former semi-finalist set to enter qualifying
Tennis.summary: Jack Draper misses out on 2026 US Open main draw as former semi-finalist set to enter qualifying Sky Sports
Tennis.body:
Former British No 1 Jack Draper is set to have to qualify for the US Open this year as the 2024 semi-finalist missed out on a spot in the main draw. Draper is poised to return to action at the DC Open in Washington from July 27 after missing Wimbledon due to a recurrence of bone bruising in his left arm.

The injury was the latest blow for the 24-year-old, who has managed only a handful of tournaments since first stepping away from the tour a year ago with the same issue. Draper's ranking has taken a hit as a result, dropping down to 147th in the world, resulting in him having to likely qualify in order to play the fourth and final Grand Slam of the season.

Tennis.title: Nearly one year after reaching No.4, Jack Draper begins rebuild from Challenger level
Tennis.summary: Nearly one year after reaching No.4, Jack Draper begins rebuild from Challenger level Yardbarker
Tennis.body:
Just a year after reaching the ATP Top 5, Jack Draper is facing one of the biggest rebuilding challenges of his career. The Briton has entered the Brownsburg Challenger, scheduled for August 10-16, as he looks to recover his ranking, confidence and competitive rhythm after a difficult period marked by injuries.

Draper’s presence at Challenger level would have been almost impossible to imagine months ago. The 24-year-old was one of the biggest rising stars in tennis, reaching a career-high No. 4 ranking and becoming a Grand Slam semifinalist before physical setbacks interrupted the momentum of a breakthrough period.

Tennis.title: How Asian brands build global rosters, one deal at a time
Tennis.summary: How Asian brands build global rosters, one deal at a time Sporting Goods Intelligence Europe
Tennis.body:
A widening roster of basketball and tennis signings, from Stephen Curry and Nikola Jokic to Kyrie Irving, Emma Navarro and Emma Raducanu, shows Anta, Li-Ning, 361 Degrees, Uniqlo and Asics building signature shoes, co-designed lines and ambassador programs across North America and Europe.

When Dwyane Wade walked away from Nike’s Jordan Brand for Li-Ning in 2012, the sports business press treated it as a curiosity, a wealthy Chinese company buying a name it could not otherwise earn (The New York Times, October 2012). Fourteen years later, that move looks less like an anomaly and more like the opening move of a strategy that has since scaled across three Chinese companies, two Japanese ones, and dozens of athletes spanning basketball, tennis and football.

Tennis.title: WTA: Tour announces mandatory SRY gene test for players to determine their sex in order to compete
Tennis.summary: WTA: Tour announces mandatory SRY gene test for players to determine their sex in order to compete Sky Sports
Tennis.body:
The WTA has announced that tennis players will have to undergo genetic sex testing to play on the women's tour. In an update to its eligibility policy, the WTA confirmed that athletes will have to undergo a one-time test for the SRY gene, which determines biological sex, coming into effect on Tuesday, with players facing disciplinary action should they refuse testing.

Previous WTA rules allowed the participation of transgender women provided their declared gender was female and they maintained a lower testosterone level for two years before competing.

Tennis.title: Players will need sex test to play on WTA Tour
Tennis.summary: The Women's Tennis Association is to ask all players to undergo genetic sex testing in order to compete on the WTA Tour.
Tennis.body:
The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) is to require all players to undergo genetic sex testing in order to compete on the WTA Tour. In the latest edition of its women's eligibility policy, which will come into effect on Tuesday, players will be required to provide a cheek swab, blood or saliva sample to test for the presence of the SRY gene which is part of the Y chromosome and causes male characteristics to develop.

Players will be tested just once in their lifetime and only a negative result, showing no presence of the gene, will permit them to compete on the Tour. If they test positive, players will face further medical assessment before being allowed to play.

Tennis.summary: Stefanos Tsitsipas wins his first ATP title in 16 months after defeating Raphael Collignon in the Swiss Open final.
Tennis.body:
Stefanos Tsitsipas has won his first ATP title in 16 months after defeating Raphael Collignon in the Swiss Open final. The former world number three and two-time Grand Slam finalist overcame the Belgian 6-4 6-7 (3-7) 6-3 to claim the 13th ATP title of his career.

Tsitsipas' last title was the Dubai Open in March 2025, where he beat Felix Auger-Aliassime in straight sets. "I would like to start by mentioning how amazing the final was today," said the Greek, who will climb from 85 to 55 in the updated world rankings on Monday.

Tennis.body:
Emma Raducanu pulled out of Wimbledon 2026 hours before her opening match after scans confirmed a stress fracture in her lower right leg. It was the latest blow in a career that has been defined more by injury bulletins than by trophies. Since her stunning 2021 US Open title, the 23-year-old has undergone wrist and ankle surgeries, missed large parts of two seasons, and is now ranked No. 38 in the world. Former British No. 1 Greg Rusedski has had enough of watching Britain's best players break down and he is pointing to

Tennis.title: West London’s Queen’s Club bids to open two new squash courts
Tennis.summary: West London’s Queen’s Club bids to open two new squash courts London Evening Standard
Tennis.body:
The two proposed courts would involve one to be designed for doubles competitions and another for exhibition singles games. If approved it will require the demolition of a series of derelict buildings as well as the redevelopment of part of Mary MacArthur House, a five-storey housing block built by the council in 1939.

The Club itself dates back to the late 1880s, with its website describing it as “the first multipurpose sports complex ever to be built, anywhere in the world”. It offers members the opportunity to play sports such as padel and squash as well as tennis and hosts the annual ATP Tour 500 and WTA 500 tournaments. This year’s singles competitions were won by Francisco Cerundolo and Donna Vekić.

Golf.title: ‘Golf needs rivalries’: Rory McIlroy's former agent believes animosity between Masters champion and Bryson DeChambeau is good for the game
Golf.summary: ‘Golf needs rivalries’: Rory McIlroy's former agent believes animosity between Masters champion and Bryson DeChambeau is good for the game Belfast Telegraph
Golf.body:
Rory McIlroy’s recent comments about Bryson DeChambeau at The Open Championship are exactly what golf needs, claims the Holywood star’s former agent Andrew ‘Chubby’ Chandler. McIlroy, in his usual forthright manner, described DeChambeau’s manner as ‘performative’ after the two-time US Open winner was involved in a rules dispute on day two at Royal Birkdale last week.

DeChambeau was assessed a two-stroke penalty for inadvertently improving his lie on the fifth hole, but it was his actions following that which drew McIlroy’s ire, the big-hitting American threatening to withdraw from the tournament in protest while also trying to get US President Donald Trump involved, which delayed the release of the third round tee times.

The 2026 U.S. Junior Amateur has moved on to match play, and so far much of the attention has been on a competitor who narrowly missed out on the final rounds: Charlie Woods. The 17-year-old son of three-time U.S. Junior Am champ Tiger Woods lost in a 14-man playoff on Wednesday for the final two spots in the match-play portion of the event. But another competitor, James Nagle, saw his hopes of a U.S. Junior Amateur triumph end much earlier. Rather than a result of his play, Nagle’s exit came in the form of a DQ on Monday, a result of breaching a rare, recently adopted rule.

Golf.title: How Ryan Fox, Shane Lowry, and Nico Echavarria choose their wedge set-ups
Golf.summary: Ryan Fox has a unique steep delivery that required the perfect RTZ grind at Royal Birkdale. Picking wedges is more about you than the ground. The post How Ryan Fox, Shane Lowry, and Nico Echavarria choose their wedge set-ups appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
When championship conditions turn baked-out and firm, the knee-jerk reaction among amateur players is to instantly strip bounce off every wedge in the bag. And YES, it did happen a bit last week at Royal Birkdale with players getting low bounce wedge grinds built up “just in case”.

The logic seems sound on paper: tighter lies demand a lower leading edge to prevent the sole from skidding into the middle of the golf ball. On Tour, however, the response from the trucks is far more personal. While firm fairways and tight turf do trigger an influx of low-bounce wedge options across the field, a player’s delivery geometry, swing path, and wrist release play a far larger role in grind selection than ground hardness alone.

Golf.title: LIV's team event on brink of cancellation, per captain Martin Kaymer
Golf.summary: "The whole season was a bit of a …" LIV captain Martin Kaymer told Today's Golfer, opening up as the league faces funding challenges. The post LIV’s team event on brink of cancellation, per captain Martin Kaymer appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Martin Kaymer, captain of LIV Golf’s Cleeks team, told reporters on Wednesday that it is “highly unlikely” the circuit will stage its August team finale in Michigan. The news was first reported by Ben Parsons of Today’s Golfer, who spoke with a “disappointed” Kaymer ahead of this week’s LIV Golf UK event.

It comes as the embattled league seeks to secure funding for next season following the withdrawal of Saudi support earlier this season. Kaymer said that he expects the next three LIV events — this week in England and subsequent events in New Jersey and Indianapolis — will go ahead as scheduled, but barring a sudden change, the team finale in Michigan, scheduled for the Cardinal at Saint John’s in Plymouth, Mich., won’t happen. (He put the chances at five percent.) An earlier event scheduled for New Orleans was postponed indefinitely.

Chief executive Scot O’Neil is leading the search for over €300million of new money after the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia announced it was withdrawing backing at the end of the year after spending almost €4bn since its inception in 2021.

O’Neil spoke to the team captains on Tuesday at this week’s LIV event in Staffordshire and two-time major winner Kaymer said the news was not particularly encouraging. "I know that Indianapolis (the final individual event) is most likely happening. There was a conversation yesterday: Michigan, highly unlikely. According to yesterday, it didn’t look good," he told reporters at the event.

Golf.title: For only $20, you can play this quirky six-time Open Championship site
Golf.summary: Musselburgh Links, a six-time Open site outside Edinburgh, Scotland, sits inside the Musselburgh Racecourse, on its sprawling infield. The post For only $20, you can play this quirky six-time Open Championship site appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
I played a new course the other day — that is, new to me — a nine-holer with a bargain-basement green fee and a wide-open tee sheet. It’s in Scotland, outside Edinburgh and inside the Musselburgh Racecourse, on its sprawling, rumpled infield. I had heard people talk about the Musselburgh Links often over the years but finally got to it a couple days after Ryan Fox, get-on-with-it Kiwi golfer, holed his winning putt at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. Fox could play this par-34 course, a former Open venue itself, in under an hour. He plays fast and so does this course. When the Scots invented golf they didn’t mean for it to be an all-day activity. (While we’re young, mon — or do your sheep shear themselves?) I imagine the new Open champ would like it. I know Sandy Lyle, winner of the ’85 Open, digs its whole vibe.

Upon arrival I saw no signs for the pro shop or whatever so I walked through an open pathway to the track itself, the red-brick grandstands now behind me, lush grass track ahead. The whole place was pretty much asleep on this warm weekday afternoon, and the whole scene brought to mind a long-ago visit to Doubleday Field in Cooperstown, N.Y., on a still summer day when there was no game.

Golf.title: Aaron Wise is battling more than just the golf course
Golf.summary: Former NCAA champ and PGA Tour Rookie of the Year Aaron Wise left golf to focus on his mental health. Now he's ready to talk about it. The post Aaron Wise is battling more than just the golf course appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
BLAINE, Minn. — Aaron Wise thinks hard before he answers questions. He wants to actually answer them, because he wants you to understand, because he’s spent years trying to make sense of it himself. His press conference at the 3M Open on Wednesday was lengthy and vulnerable and thoughtful. He had a lot to say. But probably because Aaron Wise has had a lot to deal with.

“It’s a constant daily battle out here,” Wise said. Years ago, Wise was one of the brightest young stars on the PGA Tour. He was the 2016 NCAA champion, and as a 21-year-old rookie shattered the scoring record at the 2018 Byron Nelson and won PGA Tour Rookie of the Year. Then, five years later, he withdrew just days before the 2023 Masters to focus on his mental health.

Golf.title: The practice habit that's hurting your golf game without knowing
Golf.summary: GOLF Top 100 Teacher Monique Thoresz explains why leaving headphones in while practicing could be hurting your game. The post The practice habit that’s hurting your golf game without knowing appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
You’ve probably seen it at your local driving range: golfers with headphones in, either taking a phone call or listening to their favorite playlist. Maybe they’re trying to relax, block out distractions, or make practice more enjoyable. While there’s nothing in the Rules of Golf that prohibits listening to music, as a coach, I recommend leaving the headphones in your bag during practice sessions.

Golf is a game that demands concentration. One of the most important skills every player needs to develop is the ability to stay focused despite distractions. On the golf course, you can’t control the conditions. There may be noise from nearby groups, changing weather, unexpected delays, or simply long periods of waiting between shots. Learning to accept those moments instead of trying to eliminate them is an essential part of becoming a better player.

With the World No. 1 in the field this week, Cavner says tournament ticket sales have already increased 25-30 percent over last year, and that’s not even including the tickets they expect to sell later this week or at the gates when the tournament begins, which is where the majority of their sales come from.

Golf.title: Ryan Fox’s speedy pace was a marvel. Should more golfers step on the gas?
Golf.summary: Watching Ryan Fox motor his way to an Open Championship victory makes you wonder if more golfers wouldn’t benefit from picking up the pace. The post Ryan Fox’s speedy pace was a marvel. Should more golfers step on the gas? appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
If you didn’t see Ryan Fox coming, that might be because relative to many of his grind-it-out, stuck-in-the-mud peers, Fox blazes around the course like a greyhound chasing a hare. Ask Scottie Scheffler, who played alongside Fox and Zecheng Dou in the third round of the Phoenix Open earlier this year — or at least Scheffler thinks he played with Fox. “We walk off the 9th tee, and he goes, ‘Foxy, it doesn’t even feel like you’re in the group,’” the newly minted Champion Golfer of the Year said Sunday evening at Birkdale. “It just feels like we’re playing in a two-ball, you hit it so fast. It’s just in the air.”

Fox has always played with haste, dating back to his teen days in Auckland, New Zealand, when he’d join his father, Grant, a New Zealand rugby great, on corporate golf outings and intentionally waste little time to ensure he wasn’t holding up his playing partners. That Fox processed things quickly — not just on the golf course but also on the cricket pitch and tennis court — also didn’t hurt. See ball, hit ball.

Golf.body:
ROCESTER, England – Whether it happens this week in the UK or next month in the U.S., Jon Rahm likely will win his third consecutive LIV Golf season-long Individual Championship. Nothing is guaranteed as of now, but it seems inevitable – as inevitable as a top-10 finish whenever Rahm tees it up at a LIV Golf tournament.

Rahm could clinch the three-peat if he wins LIV Golf United Kingdom presented by JCB, provided his closest pursuer, Bryson DeChambeau, doesn’t finish solo second or in a two-way tie for second. If DeChambeau finishes in a three-way tie for second or worse, then Rahm would have enough points going into the final two regular-season tournaments in New York and Indianapolis to clinch the title, no matter what anybody else does.

Golf.title: 2 major pro golf acquisitions just gave us a glimpse into the future
Golf.summary: On an otherwise innocuous Tuesday, two major pro golf announcements provided a glimpse into golf's competitive future. The post 2 major pro golf acquisitions just gave us a glimpse into the future appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Changes to professional golf in the LIV era, while frequent, are about as interesting as bowel movements. I get it because I have also felt my eyes glaze over at a headline capturing the “latest changes.” I get it because I have also wondered when and how much I am supposed to care about the smallest shifts in corporate governance and marketing budgets. I get it because I have also felt a vague annoyance with the fact that this news cycle develops in a thousand small drips rather than a single, steady stream of information.

As a reporter, it is my job to care about these things — and I’ve felt that way. I can only imagine where that leaves you. But some changes in golf are significant not for what they are but for what they represent. That’s the category the two changes filed on Tuesday morning fit into in the golf world: The PGA Tour’s expanded strategic alliance with the DP World Tour and Asian Tour; and the LPGA’s decision to play an event in Hawaii at what might be considered the best golf course on the islands, Nanea.

Golf.title: Cam Young's top tip for amateurs is one he still uses himself
Golf.summary: In this episode of Warming Up, Cameron Young explains that the most common advice he gives to amateurs is also the simplest. The post Cam Young’s top tip for amateurs is one he still uses himself appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Once you’ve caught the golf bug, you’ll try just about anything to get better. One week, it’s a viral swing drill. The next, you’re making practice swings in the living room or staying up late studying your favorite tour player’s swing on YouTube.

While it’s tempting to believe that one swing thought can change everything, the reality is that better golf is usually built on the less glamorous work. It’s a lesson PGA Tour pros understand better than anyone. While their swings may look effortless to us mere mortals, the game’s best players are constantly working on the basics. Just ask Cameron Young.

ROCESTER, England – Ian Poulter has 17 career professional wins spread across 12 different countries. Surprisingly, he’s never won a pro tournament in his home country of England.

He has fellow Majesticks Golf Club Co-Captain Lee Westwood partially to blame. Poulter and Westwood entered the final round of the 2007 British Masters at The Belfry tied for second behind fellow Englishman Mark Foster. Westwood ended up winning the title with a superb final-round 65 while Poulter’s 70 left him in solo second.

Golf.title: A global golf shakeup has the Asian Tour partnering with the PGA Tour, DP World Tour—and leaving behind LIV Golf
Golf.summary: A global golf shakeup has the Asian Tour partnering with the PGA Tour, DP World Tour—and leaving behind LIV Golf Golf Digest
Golf.body:
Asian Tour CEO and Commissioner Cho Minn Thant says a new deal with the PGA Tour and DP World Tour will provide important pathways for his members. The Asian Tour is set to re-align with the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour in a formal partnership underlined by pathways and co-sanctioned tournaments, a move that means it will no longer act as LIV Golf’s important second tier.

The Asian Tour had partnered with LIV in 2021 before the league’s launch in 2022, when it created a lucrative group of tournaments called the International Series, which LIV golfers frequently teed up in. The series was central to the promotion and relegation element of LIV Golf, including the top two on its Order of Merit being promoted to LIV for the 2026 season.

Golf.title: Team Power Rankings: LIV Golf UK Presented by JCB
Golf.summary: Team Power Rankings: LIV Golf UK Presented by JCB LIV Golf
Golf.body:
Legion XIII is the hottest team entering this week, but there are plenty of others who are trending nicely as the action nears at JCB Golf & Country Club. As the LIV Golf League heads to JCB Golf & Country Club for LIV Golf United Kingdom Presented by JCB, the stage is set for the 10th stop on the schedule. Last year, Torque GC Captain Joaquin Niemann claimed the individual title with a three-shot victory over RangeGoats Golf Club Captain Bubba Watson, while Legion XIII took home the team trophy.

JCB Golf & Country Club will host the event for the third time. The par-72, 7,332-yard course opened in 2018 and was designed by Robin Hiseman. The 17th is the signature hole, a 255-yard par-3 that sits on a converted island and has the potential to play a crucial role when the leaders come down the stretch. If that wasn’t difficult enough, the 18th features a green heavily guarded by four intimidating bunkers, while the three-tier putting surface could see many players face difficult two-putts to finish their rounds.

Golf.title: Rules Guy: I abandoned my lost ball — then found it in the hole! What now?
Golf.summary: What do you do if you give up on looking for your tee shot, only to later find it in the hole? Rules Guy has the answer. The post Rules Guy: I abandoned my lost ball — then found it in the hole! What now? appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
The Rules of Golf are tricky! Thankfully, we’ve got the guru. Our Rules Guy knows the book front to back. Got a question? He’s got all the answers. During a friendly 4-ball, teeing off on a blind par-4, my playing partner could not find her tee shot. The group searched for more than 3 minutes for her ball. My partner decided to “pick up” rather than head back to the tee. Soon enough, another player in the group checked the hole for fun — no one had thought to look there, since it was a par-4 … and there it was. A hole-in-one! But was it really, given the circumstances? – Teresa White, Purchase, NY

Really, it was, even if it sounds like the group didn’t get the free round of drinks owed at the 19th hole. Your partner indeed made a hole-in-one — and, even rarer, an albatross to boot! The fact that the ball wasn’t found in the search time didn’t matter, nor did her “picking up,” because she had already completed the hole. Rule 6.5, “Completing Play of a Hole,” completely covers this situation.

Golf.body:
Bryson DeChambeau has been accused of threatening to call Donald Trump during a row with senior R&A officials on Friday after the American golfer was handed a two-shot penalty at the Open.

DeChambeau’s alleged use of the US president’s name as he argued his case marks the latest bizarre turn in what was already the dominant story of the 2026 Open. DeChambeau was handed a two-stroke penalty for improving the line of his swing by standing on long grass behind his ball on Royal Birkdale’s fifth hole during round two. The 32-year-old argued his case furiously, including insisting upon returning to the scene of the incident with the R&A’s head of governance and a senior referee.

Golf.title: Cameron Young's patented pause? Here's why he does it
Golf.summary: In a recent episode of Warming Up, Cameron Young explained to Dylan Dethier the origins of his pause at the top of the backswing. The post Cameron Young’s patented pause? Here’s why he does it appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Cameron Young’s ball striking is perhaps his greatest asset as a golfer. Since graduating to the PGA Tour in 2022, the 29-year-old pro has ranked inside the top 35 in SG: Off the Tee every season and has twice ranked inside the top 15 in SG: Tee to Green. This season, as his putter has heated up to complement his lethal ball striking, he’s had a career year, winning the Players Championship and finishing top five in two majors.

Young’s swing is certainly effective, but it also comes with its own idiosyncrasies. Chief among them is the slight pause he makes at the top of his backswing. “I don’t feel it, obviously,” Young said in a recent episode of Warming Up. “It looks like it hangs there more than it does.”

Commentating on the thrilling climax of this year's Open, there was barely a moment to describe the biggest putt of Ryan Fox's life because he struck it so quickly. There were only 22 seconds between Sam Burns completing his final round and Fox stroking home the 11-footer on Royal Birkdale's 18th green. The putt made him champion golfer of the year.

It provided a magnificent and wholesome climax to the 154th Open, a dramatic championship marked by class and controversy. Bryson DeChambeau's two-shot penalty for trampling rough that improved the line of his swing path last Friday will not be forgotten. It was another incident that illustrated why he has become golf's most divisive figure.

Golf.title: Inside Cam Young’s 2 hours of belief … and 1 heartbreaking moment
Golf.summary: Cameron Young sat in the clubhouse and watched the Open Championship fall into his lap. In an instant it was snatched away. The post Inside Cam Young’s 2 hours of belief … and 1 heartbreaking moment appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Kyle Sterbinsky stood on the far left side of the Open Championship driving range and looked … warm. The sun seemed to canvas his entire face as he stared off in the distance at the big, golden leaderboard maybe 250 yards away. He couldn’t have been scanning the scene for info because his eyes were no longer useful. He and Cameron Young, the star golfer he caddies for, had reached those pregnant seconds when golf history is made. All they could do was listen.

There are two schools of thought that arise on Sundays at golf tournaments. Either you want to be the man in the house — shoes off, hat backwards, watching how your score holds up — or you want the ball and holes to play to beat the man in the house.
Golf.copy:
SOUTHPORT, England — Kyle Sterbinsky stood on the far left side of the Open Championship driving range and looked … warm. The sun seemed to canvas his entire face as he stared off in the distance at the big, golden leaderboard maybe 250 yards away. He couldn’t have been scanning the scene for info because his eyes were no longer useful. He and Cameron Young, the star golfer he caddies for, had reached those pregnant seconds when golf history is made. All they could do was listen.

There are two schools of thought that arise on Sundays at golf tournaments. Either you want to be the man in the house — shoes off, hat backwards, watching how your score holds up — or you want the ball and holes to play to beat the man in the house.

Golf.title: Pantomime villain Bryson DeChambeau ends his Open with a whimper | Sean Ingle
Golf.summary: Pantomime villain Bryson DeChambeau ends his Open with a whimper | Sean Ingle The Guardian
Golf.body:
Deep into the final round of the Open, and Bryson DeChambeau is almost legless in the last chance saloon. He has slipped to minus five, four off the clubhouse lead, with eight holes to play. Worse still, he has not made birdie all day. But there is a sliver of hope. After all, in 2017, Jordan Spieth made up four shots on the back nine here to take the Claret Jug. History couldn’t repeat itself, could it?

The loyal band of Brysonites cheer as he steps on to the tricky par-four 11th, and takes out a driver. Yet they, and Royal Birkdale’s infamous rough, are about to turn viciously against him.

Scottie Scheffler told “Brucey” and “Woody” to stop looking. And with that, the four-time major winner found one of the wildest rules breaks you’ll see, and in the deciding moments of the Open Championship, no less.

Golf.title: Tommy Fleetwood's home Open had a different dream ending
Golf.summary: Tommy Fleetwood's dream home Open at Royal Birkdale didn't end with a Claret Jug. Instead, it closed with a scene that meant something deeper. The post Tommy Fleetwood’s home Open had a different dream ending appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Tommy Fleetwood has had a dream for his entire life. He has seen it when he’s closed his eyes, and he has envisioned it in quiet moments on and off the golf course. There’s a term for the space in between sleep and awake. It’s called hypnopompia, the state of near-consciousness in which dreams and reality blur, producing momentary lucid visions. Put simply, it’s a brief moment when you are living your dreams.

Tommy Fleetwood never fell asleep this week at his home Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. But he didn’t need to feel like he was living out a dream he’d long conjured in his mind. He just wasn’t sure how his dream would end.

Golf.title: Winners and Losers from 2026 Open Championship Sunday
Golf.summary: Where did this Open's cast of characters finish up, from Ryan Fox to Bryson DeChambeau to Rory McIlroy, Cameron Young, pot bunkers and more? The post Winners and Losers from 2026 Open Championship Sunday appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
If you’re of the Ricky Bobby school of thought (if you’re not first, you’re last) you could come away from Royal Birkdale seeing just one winner and 155 losers. But we’re slightly more charitable than that — so let’s review a smattering of winners, losers and in-betweeners from what was (gulp) the final men’s major of the year.

Open champ Ryan Fox said in his post-win presser that he “sees things fast.” He plays that way, too: Quick, relentless, committed. As he said it: “It’s not that difficult to pick a shot and pick a club.”

Golf.title: Sam Burns' latest major close call hints at what's to come
Golf.summary: Sam Burns just wrapped up the best major season of his career, and all these close calls could add up to something special. The post Sam Burns’ latest major close call hints at what’s to come appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Sam Burns, Scottie’s bud. They play practice rounds together at all your better stops, speak the same language (golf, Southern, Southern golf), married young and had kids young. Burns, like Scheffler, is all church-on-Sunday, plus takeout shakes and whatever else is in the bag. You could see the two of them driving together to Brackenridge Park for the Texas Open, except that the tourney hasn’t been played there since Eisenhower was president. Scottie turned 30 on Father’s Day, last day of the U.S. Open. Burns turns 30 next week. They both seem about a decade short of playing in their first Senior British Open. Burns will be a lifer. You can just tell. According to the guy who won here Sunday night, Ryan Fox, he’ll be a major winner, too.

Burns would not have come here at all, to this posh nook of gritty northwestern England, but the missus, Caroline, pushed him out of the house and into a jet. He was talking about staying home, what with a new-born baby in the crib, in the Burns family home in a little town about an hour’s drive from Shreveport, La. “I’ve got this at home,” wife told hub. “Go over there and give it your best.”

Golf.title: DeChambeau is not a cheater
Golf.summary: World number one Scottie Scheffler insists Bryson DeChambeau is "definitely not a cheater" as the rules incident which overshadowed The Open rumbles on.
Golf.body:
World number one Scottie Scheffler insists Bryson DeChambeau is "definitely not a cheater" as the discussion about the rules incident which overshadowed The Open rumbles on. DeChambeau was given a two-shot penalty after Friday's second round when he was judged to have inadvertently improved his swing path on the fifth hole.

Officials from the R&A, which organises The Open, said DeChambeau broke rules by trampling down knee-high rough behind his ball. The R&A emphasised that DeChambeau's actions had been accidental but pointed out that the rule still applied.

Golf.title: Why Ryan Fox was the perfect winner for a strange Open week
Golf.summary: Ryan Fox won the Open Championship, ending a strange and controversial week at Royal Birkdale with a good-guy winner. The post Why Ryan Fox was the perfect winner for a strange Open week appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Golf, it’s a beautiful thing. A year ago, the No. 1 player in the world went wire-to-wire at the Open Championship to claim a blowout victory. On Sunday, a little-known, 39-year-old PGA Tour lifer with just three career victories claimed his first solo lead of the week on the 72nd hole with a birdie putt for golfing immortality.

And best of all? He waited just 22 seconds to hit it. Ryan Fox was not the victor the scriptwriters had in mind for this 154th Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. In fact, he might arrive in the winner’s circle as the most compelling evidence against the scriptwriters, beating out hometown kid Tommy Fleetwood and major-winner-in-waiting Cam Young and new-dad Sam Burns en route to his narrative-altering win.

Golf.title: Open fans provide valuable lesson with Bryson DeChambeau treatment
Golf.summary: Would Open fans give Bryson DeChambeau the same type of treatment Wyndham Clark received at the U.S. Open? No, not even close. The post Open fans provide valuable lesson with Bryson DeChambeau treatment appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — You might have been wondering: Would Bryson DeChambeau be to this 154th British Open what Wyndham Clark was to the 118th U.S. Open, last month at Shinnecock Hills? You know, the player fans love to abuse?

This boils it down to the bone and then some, but if you’re looking at their original sins, there are similarities. Clark’s original crime was to bash in a locker at Oakmont Country Club, site of the 2025 U.S. Open, the premier annual event of the USGA. DeChambeau’s was stomping all over the deep fescue rough, right behind his ball, on the right side of the fifth hole, here at Royal Birkdale, site of this year’s Open Championship, premier annual event of the R&A. These were not acts, and these were not actors, out of the Bobby Jones/Jack Nicklaus Establishment Golfer playbooks. Like, the total opposite.

Golf.title: 4 things you didn't know about Open Championship winner Ryan Fox
Golf.summary: Ryan Fox is your 2026 Champion Golfer of the Year. Here's what you need to know about the 39-year-old from New Zealand. The post 4 things you didn’t know about Open Championship winner Ryan Fox appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Ryan Fox is officially your Champion Golfer of the Year. Fox, who started the day two shots back of Sam Burns’ 54-hole lead, posted a final-round 68 at Royal Birkdale to post 10-under and earn his first major title at the Open Championship. His round included birdies on four of his final six holes — including a 3 at the last to clinch the title — as he becomes just the third man from New Zealand to win a major championship.

Entering the week, few had Fox on their shortlist of contenders at the year’s final major. But after 72 holes of spectacular golf (including a record-tying 62 on Saturday) he will be immortalized forever with his name engraved on the Claret Jug.

Golf.summary: In the aftermath of his stunning Open win, Ryan Fox had an emotional call with his wife and young daughters back home. The post Ryan Fox’s emotional phone call with family after Open win appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
The 2026 Open Championship finished in dramatic fashion on Sunday, with 39-year-old Ryan Fox birdieing four of Royal Birkdale’s final six holes — including the 18th, which required an 11-foot birdie putt to get him to 10 under par overall, avoiding a playoff with clubhouse leader Cameron Young — to claim the year’s final major title outright by a single shot.

The win marked the first major championship of Fox’s career, but he has been a world-class player for more than a decade, with eight international victories between 2014 and 2023, and two on the PGA Tour, both of which were last year: the 2025 RBC Canadian Open and the 2025 ONEflight Myrtle Beach Classic.

Golf.title: Fleetwood won't give up Open dream after 'special' week
Golf.summary: Tommy Fleetwood says he will continue to chase his dream of winning The Open after falling short at the end of a "special week" on home soil at Royal Birkdale.
Golf.body:
Tommy Fleetwood says he will continue to chase his dream of winning The Open after falling short at the end of a "special week" on home soil at Royal Birkdale. Hoping to clinch his first major and become the first Englishman to lift the Claret Jug since Nick Faldo in 1992, Fleetwood started the final round five shots back of overnight leader Sam Burns.

Roared on by huge crowds, Fleetwood birdied three of his first eight holes to vault into contention before a hat-trick of bogeys around the turn wrecked his chances. "[Walking down] 18 was pretty emotional," said Fleetwood, who carded a final-round 68 to finish seven under and three shots adrift of winner Ryan Fox.

As chaos unfolded on Sunday afternoon at the 154th Open Championship, Ryan Fox was the man who kept cool in the baking conditions at Royal Birkdale. The 39-year-old New Zealander, who is the son of All Black rugby legend Grant, shot a two-under 68 to finish one ahead of American Cameron Young and lift the Claret Jug.

After a final round full of spills and thrills, Fox knew a birdie on the 18th would be enough to secure his first major title. Easier said than done. The long par-four had yielded only four birdies all day, but the courageous Fox did not take a step back as he chased down long-time clubhouse leader Young.

Golf.summary: New Zealand's Ryan Fox birdied the 18th hole at Royal Birkdale to win the 2026 Open Championship and claim his first major title. The post Ryan Fox wins Open Championship, claims first major in shocking fashion appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Cameron Young shot 64 on Sunday at Royal Birkdale, and then he waited. And waited. And waited some more. He started the day seven back but now held the clubhouse lead, although surely the hole he started in was simply too big a deficit to overcome and win the Open Championship, right?

But the longer he waited — it became over two hours — the longer it seemed like a possibility he would hoist the Claret Jug. The 39-year-old New Zealander, ranked 56th in the World, birdied two of his last three holes, including the par-4 18th, to clip Young by one and claim the biggest title of his career.

Golf.body:
Last year, the Open Championship purse took a break from a steady annual uptick that began in 2017, opting to hold the line at $17 million. But this year, an increase is back. The 2026 Open Championship purse has gone up by $750,000 to $17.75 million.

Golf.title: With major season over, Rory McIlroy's changing PGA Tour feelings take center stage

Golf.body:
Rory McIlroy’s major season ended on Sunday with a whimper. The reigning back-to-back Masters champion shot a final-round one-over 71 at Royal Birkdale to finish in a tie for 40th at this Open Championship.

With his 2026 major season in the books, the six-time major champion looked to the future — but not with both eyes on the PGA Tour. “Look, this season feels very similar to last season,” McIlroy said. “Obviously won the first major of the year, fell off a little bit after that, but still any time you win a major in a year, you have to be pleased about that. Yeah, like I haven’t really took the time to enjoy that or celebrate that. Poppy’s got another four weeks off school until she goes back, sort of middle to end of August, so just going to enjoy the summer holidays with her and Erica. Yeah, that’s what I’m looking forward to the most.

Golf.title: Rory McIlroy Comments On Bryson DeChambeau As Performative At The Open
Golf.summary: Rory McIlroy Comments On Bryson DeChambeau As Performative At The Open Forbes
Golf.body:
During Rory McIlroy’s Saturday press conference following his third round at The Open Championship, McIlroy was asked about Bryson DeChambeau’s two-shot penalty assessed after Friday’s round. “Yeah, look, I won’t pretend to be up here and defend Bryson,”, said McIlroy. “I’m not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it’s performative. I think a lot of it’s for attention.

“To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn’t feel like it was a great look.” McIlroy’s comments came after DeChambeau was assessed a two-shot penalty following Friday’s round. After his tee shot sailed right on the fifth hole on Friday, DeChambeau found himself in a penalty area in waist-high fescue grass. Instead of taking a drop, he elected to play his ball as it lay. However, as DeChambeau was lining up his shot, he stepped on and around the grass behind his ball. He struck the shot, ending up behind the green and eventually making a bogey on the hole.

DeChambeau bogeyed the hole, but rallied from there and believed he had shot a 66 and was at 7 under par for the tournament, one behind leader Lucas Herbert.

Golf.title: Tommy Fleetwood keeps dreaming. So does everyone at Birkdale
Golf.summary: Tommy Fleetwood's dreams are playing out at the Open Championship. On Sunday, they'll mean something completely different. The post Tommy Fleetwood keeps dreaming. So does everyone at Birkdale appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — There’s a popular phrase in golf that says there are no pictures on scorecards; just numbers. It’s all about the integers written and the sums they create. The phrase is popular because it’s true most of the time.

Just not on Saturday for Tommy Fleetwood in the town where he was raised. We needed pictures on the scorecard, because 18 holes came and went and, somehow, he’s one shot further away from the Open Championship lead (5) than when his day began (4). And because that score tells us precisely nothing about one of the most thrilling scenes pro golf can make. Royal Birkdale is blanketed by dreamers.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau fallout a reminder that game should always come first
Golf.summary: Arnold Palmer’s grandson is not claiming he knows what his grandfather would say about the Bryson DeChambeau uproar, but he offered a guess. The post Bryson DeChambeau fallout a reminder that game should always come first appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Bryson loved Arnold. He has said that more than once. Oh, where are my manners here, especially for you young people? Arnold Palmer, who won the first of his two British Opens here at Royal Birkdale in 1961. Bryson, of course, is Bryson DeChambeau, winner of the 2021 Arnold Palmer Invitational, about 15 months before he went LIV. Bryson won Arnold’s event, put on a red cardigan emblematic of the late host and said that Arnold would be in his dream foursome, along with Ben Hogan and his father. Nice.

On Friday night, here at Royal Birkdale, DeChambeau found himself in a rules dispute with the R&A, presenters of this oldest of golf tournaments, the Open Championship, and, with the USGA, the writers of its rules and the final arbiter of its rules disputes. Almost every player with a long career has eventually had one or more rules disputes with golf’s officialdom. Arnold certainly did. How you handle them is how you handle them.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau plays to the gallery whether or not they think he is villain or victim | Andy Bull
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau plays to the gallery whether or not they think he is villain or victim | Andy Bull The Guardian
Golf.body:
Whip, crack, whoosh, Bryson DeChambeau’s opening shot flies into the distance, pitches, skips, and tumbles into the rough left of the fairway. By the time DeChambeau has reached the ball a big crowd has gathered around it, they’re standing on tiptoes, perched on mounds, tilting sideways to peer around the people in front, who are pressed right up against the ropes and even spilling underneath them and on to the playing area where the marshals, hands out, are trying to usher them back.

“Careful Bryson!” someone shouts out as he wades into the rough and, it never takes much, everyone breaks out laughing. Looking around, you notice how many people are watching all this through their phones. I start counting: one, five, 10, 20, 50 – people don’t just want to see DeChambeau play golf, they want to be able to show everyone they know that they’ve done it. Did you even go to the Open if you didn’t get to see him?

Golf.title: British Open 2026: The day after scandal, Bryson DeChambeau was a mix of power and pantomime
Golf.summary: British Open 2026: The day after scandal, Bryson DeChambeau was a mix of power and pantomime Golf Digest
Golf.body:
1. The children love Bryson. In the time I spent following Bryson DeChambeau in his third round at the Open Championship, just one child was guilty of punk-ish predilections, and I only heard about the kid secondhand—apparently, the precocious little snot-nosed guttersnipe shouted "watch your step!" as Bryson walked past the range. I can confirm that this was an anomaly. The rest of the kids were clamoring for autographs, and selfies, and high-fives, and he granted as many as he could. The engine of this affection was clear enough from the kid who asked him if he was going to "break 50" that day, referring to an ongoing series on his YouTube channel. The Internet charm offensive has worked.

2. The adults at Royal Birkdale mostly liked Bryson too … other than Rory McIlroy. After the bizarre scene Friday night when he was assessed a two-stroke penalty and seemed to flirt with the idea of withdrawing completely, they greeted him throughout his front nine by shouting his name or some variation thereof—"De-Beau" was popular—and even in the rare moments when they dogged him in their lilting Scouse accents, it was pretty tame stuff.

Golf.title: Winners and Losers from Open Championship Saturday
Golf.summary: Rory McIlroy and Bryson DeChambeau stole headlines on Open Saturday, while an unlikely cast of characters gathered atop the leaderboard. The post Winners and Losers from Open Championship Saturday appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
They say the Open Championship doesn’t start until you get your Saturday tee time (nobody says this), but thanks to a series of strange Bryson DeChambeau-related events, that took a bit longer this time around.

But once things started happening, they just kept happening. Here’s a mix of good and bad from the third round at Royal Birkdale. That would be the ninth tee time of the day, the early twosome of Xander Schauffele and Ryan Fox, who combined for 15 birdies in a morning Birkdale beatdown. Schauffele shot four-under 66 in what has become his customary weekend charge at a major championship — and he still lost by four to Fox, who became this week’s third 62-shooter and just the eighth in major history.

Golf.title: The simple swing thought that led to this pro's unlikely Open win
Golf.summary: On GOLF's Subpar podcast, 2004 Open champ Todd Hamilton detailed the tiny tweak he made before his improbable win at Royal Troon. The post The simple swing thought that led to this pro’s unlikely Open win appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Todd Hamilton’s victory at the 2004 Open Championship surprised a lot of people, including him. Heading into the event, Hamilton was a little-known journeyman who’d spent more than a decade on the Japan Golf Tour. After trying — and failing — eight times to earn his PGA Tour card, he finally made the big stage in 2003, at age 38.

In early 2004, Hamilton captured his first Tour title at the Honda Classic. But the week before the Open, he wasn’t at his best, posting a middling finish at the John Deere Classic. His cross-Atlantic trip didn’t bode well either. Delayed while connecting through Chicago, Hamilton arrived at Royal Troon late Tuesday afternoon, leaving little time to prepare. In his opening round, he ground out a 71, birdieing the last for an even-par round, which put him in a better frame of mind.

Golf.title: All that Royal Birkdale brown? Meet the guy (and dog) in charge of it
Golf.summary: Sean McLean, Royal Birkdale’s course manager, will tell you that brown is the great color of linksland golf. The post All that Royal Birkdale brown? Meet the guy (and dog) in charge of it appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — In a bustling R&A tent Friday afternoon, at tea/beer/toasty time, two Scotsmen with deep connections to Royal Birkdale were having a wee chat. The older gent, Alastair Johnston, wearing a tailored linen sport coat, was talking about a man he knew well, Arnold Palmer, winner of the 1961 British Open at Royal Birkdale. Johnston managed Palmer’s business affairs for more than four years. The younger man, Sean McLean, wearing shorts and sneakers and a workingman’s golf shirt, was all ears. McLean knew the precise location of the plaque at Birkdale that memorializes the 6-iron Palmer hit from thick rough near a bush en route to winning here 65 years ago. McLean is the course manager here.

McLean’s joy — from this chance meeting with one of golf’s secret legends, from this lovely July afternoon, from the rugged grandeur of this 154th Open, from this unique life in greenkeeping (and brownkeeping) he has made for himself — was inspiring. When McLean worked in the United States, at Southern Hills and Oak Hill, among other places, the term of art was superintendent. When he got the top job at Birkdale, succeeding another secret legend of the game, Chris Whittle, he was assigned a title, course manager. But the term he prefers is greenkeeper, no s. Old Tom Morris was a greenkeeper. A keeper of the green. The green was the course, all of it, as in the phrase through the green.

Golf.title: ‘Not particularly fond of him’: Rory McIlroy rips Bryson DeChambeau at Open
Golf.summary: Rory McIlroy, in response to Bryson DeChambeau’s rules controversy, ripped him at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. The post ‘Not particularly fond of him’: Rory McIlroy rips Bryson DeChambeau at Open appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Rory McIlroy, when asked about Bryson DeChambeau’s Open Championship rules controversy, says it was “pretty obvious” why DeChambeau was penalized and criticized his reaction. “Yeah, look, I won’t pretend to be up here and defend Bryson,” McIlroy said. “I’m not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it’s performative. I think a lot of it’s for attention.

“To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn’t feel like it was a great look.” McIlroy’s comments came Saturday after his Open third round, one round after DeChambeau was penalized two strokes for his actions in the fescue grass to the right of Royal Birkdale’s 5th hole. DeChambeau had found his ball in that area after a wayward tee shot and, as he measured how to play it, stepped on and around the grass before hitting his second shot. USA Network cameras showed the sequence, and after the round, rules officials questioned whether DeChambeau, in maneuvering, had improved the area around the ball, which isn’t allowed under Rule 8.1b of the Rules of Golf.

Golf.title: A third 62 at Birkdale
Golf.summary: New Zealand's Ryan Fox says it will be "cool" to be in the mix on Sunday after shooting an eight-under-par 62 on Saturday at Royal Birkdale.
Golf.body:
You wait nine years for a round of 62 in the Open and three come along in little over 24 hours. Early on Saturday, New Zealand's Ryan Fox carded an eight-under-par 62 in the third round at Royal Birkdale, to match the efforts of Lucas Herbert and Sam Burns on Friday and equal the lowest round in men's major history.

Fox, like Herbert, had the chance to shoot 61, but after finding the bunker off the tee on the 18th, left himself a 48-foot putt for a place in history. His attempt pulled up five feet short of the hole but he knocked that in to record the eighth round of 62 in a major championship, with half of those coming at Royal Birkdale.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau’s polarizing penalty was bold-faced message to all golfers
Golf.summary: What the R&A did with Bryson DeChambeau was issue a message to all golfers: Treat your ball and its surrounds with the respect it deserves. The post Bryson DeChambeau’s polarizing penalty was bold-faced message to all golfers appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Your response to Bryson DeChambeau’s walk on the wild side likely says more about how you feel about Bryson than your knowledge of Rule 8.1a. Would the R&A have given a two-stroke penalty to Rory McIlroy (former winner of the Open Championship) or Tommy Fleetwood (native son of these parts)? No. They are beloved figures, ’round here. Each, in his own way, flies the flag of golf’s most traditional values, ones the R&A holds dear.

Bryson DeChambeau does not. LIV Golf does not. All that look-at-me stuff on YouTube does not. The Rules of Golf seek to remove emotion and turn every situation to a binary matter: within the rules, or not. In real life, with real people on the stage, that cannot be done, try as you might.

Golf.title: What it was like as Bryson DeChambeau's controversial Open ruling unfolded

Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — The last steps of Bryson DeChambeau’s Friday evening went exactly as he would have wanted. While in contention at the Open Championship, he signed autographs, took selfies with his fans and, yes, even discussed a video collab with British YouTube golfers.

The sun had long set on Royal Birkdale and for a brief moment you might have even forgotten that his previous two hours hadn’t completely thrown this tournament on its side. DeChambeau had spent the afternoon roiling the crowd into a frenzy, not too dissimilar to the scenes from two summers ago at the U.S. Open at Pinehurst. He drove it magnificently, angled to the crowd for club selection advice on tee boxes and routinely went out of his way to high-five anyone with an open palm in sight.

Golf.title: Is Bryson DeChambeau playing Open after controversy? He takes to social media
Golf.summary: Is Bryson DeChambeau playing the Open Championship this weekend following a rules controversy on Friday? He posted to social media. The post Is Bryson DeChambeau playing Open after controversy? He takes to social media appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Bryson DeChambeau’s social media accounts, at about midnight Saturday in England, shared posts that appeared to signal the two-time major winner will play the Open Championship’s third round following a rules controversy on Friday.

“Onto the weekend…” his Instagram account posted, along with eight pictures — two of which addressed an incident that penalized DeChambeau two strokes, along with putting his status in doubt for the weekend at the major championship being played at Royal Birkdale in England. On X, DeChambeau’s account wrote: “Obviously disappointed with the ruling. I don’t agree with it, but it is what it is. This fires me up. Onto the weekend. Let’s get it.”

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau's Open Championship rules controversy, explained
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau was given a two-shot penalty during the second round of the 2026 Open Championship for violating Rule 8.1a. The post Bryson DeChambeau’s Open Championship rules controversy, explained appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Bryson DeChambeau dominated the headlines on Friday at Royal Birkdale. Unfortunately for him, it was for all the wrong reasons. Shortly after finishing his second round, DeChambeau entered the scoring tent to put a signature on the card to finalize his four-under 66. Instead, Open Championship officials alerted him that there were questions about if he’d improved his lie when preparing to hit his second shot on the par-4 fifth hole earlier in the day.

Eventually, tournament officials shuttled DeChambeau out to the scene of the incident to tell his side of the events. But despite a spirited debate with R&A officials, DeChambeau was assessed a two-stroke penalty, dropping him from seven under to five under for the championship, leaving him three back of Lucas Herbert’s lead.

Golf.body:
Bryson DeChambeau was controversially handed a two-shot penalty after shooting a 66 which had catapulted him into second place in The Open. The two-time major champion was adjudged to have improved his stance as he attempted to escape from the rough earlier in his round.

However, moments after signing his card he was informed there were issues with how he played the driveable par-four fifth and was taken out to the spot of the alleged infringement while the later finishers were still out on the course.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau threatens WD after controversial, chaotic Open penalty
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau was assessed a two-shot penalty at the Open Championship late on Friday, throwing the event into chaos. The post Bryson DeChambeau threatens WD after controversial, chaotic Open penalty appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
The first Open Championship was played in 1860, back when Queen Victoria held the throne and Charles Dickens was driving page views. One hundred and fifty-three editions of the championship have been conducted since that inaugural event; that’s a lot of golf, a lot of champion golfers of the year and a lot of consequential rulings — though few rulings that rivaled the one R&A officials adjudicated in the waning moments of the second round at Royal Birkdale on Friday.

When Bryson DeChambeau, who attracts drama like light does moths, arrived in the scorer’s cabin to sign for what he thought was a second-round, four-under 66 that had propelled him into solo second, at seven under, just one off Lucas Herbert’s lead, officials alerted DeChambeau that there was a problem. Video had surfaced of DeChambeau preparing to play his second shot in the fescue right of the fairway at the par-4 5th, and it didn’t look good.

Golf.title: Jon Rahm receives code-of-conduct warning for tomahawking club
Golf.summary: Jon Rahm received a code-of-conduct warning for spiking his golf club after an errant tee shot during the Open Championship on Friday. The post Jon Rahm receives code-of-conduct warning for tomahawking club appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Golf’s code-of-conduct policy has now come into play for a second consecutive men’s major. The latest incident involved Jon Rahm, during his second round of the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale on Friday.

Three under for the tournament and playing the par-3 15th hole, Rahm missed the green well left and tomahawked his iron onto the tee box, the club bouncing hard off the firm turf. Rahm chipped on and made bogey.

Bryson DeChambeau says he disagrees with the decision to give him a two-shot penalty during the second round of The Open at Royal Birkdale. The American looked to have lifted himself to one shot off the lead on Friday - finishing seven under par with a four-under 66 - but was whisked away by officials when he walked off the course to discuss a rules infringement.

DeChambeau was accused of trampling on long grass close to his ball on the fifth hole. After a long discussion with R&A rules officials - who run The Open - it was confirmed he had been given a two-shot penalty for "inadvertently improving his lie", pushing him back to five under par and three shots behind leader Lucas Herbert.

Golf.title: 3 simple steps for hitting more consistent chip shots
Golf.summary: GOLF Top 100 Teacher Joe Hallett has three simple keys you can rely on to hit more consistent chip shots around the greens. The post 3 simple steps for hitting more consistent chip shots appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Every golfer has experienced the feeling. One day you’re clipping crisp chip shots that finish in tap-in range, and the next you’re wondering where that touch disappeared to. Whether you’re struggling around the greens or simply looking for a dependable technique to simplify your short game, having a reliable reset can make all the difference.

Golf.title: He was a top Open favorite. After missed cut, he bemoans bad links luck at Birkdale
Golf.summary: Matt Fitzpatrick arrived as an Open favorite. He missed the cut at Royal Birkdale and bemoaned bad links luck on the way out. The post He was a top Open favorite. After missed cut, he bemoans bad links luck at Birkdale appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Matt Fitzpatrick has been one of the best golfers in the world this year. He arrived at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale with three wins under his belt in 2026 and was coming off a tie for third at the Genesis Scottish Open. Combine all that with his tie for fourth at last year’s Open at Royal Portrush, and Fitzpatrick was one of the trendiest picks to win this Open Championship.

But after back-to-back rounds of 72, Fitzpatrick will not play the weekend at Royal Birkdale, finishing with a two-day score of four-over to miss his first cut of the season. After signing his scorecard, Fitzpatrick briefly chatted with the media, pointing to bad links-golf luck and not poor play as the reason his major season will end in disappointing fashion.

Golf.title: Two record-equalling 62s at The Open
Golf.summary: Australia's Lucas Herbert and Sam Burns of the United States both shoot eight-under 62s to equal the lowest rounds in men's major history.
Golf.body:
In the space of about 20 minutes, two players added to men's major golf history at Royal Birkdale - but the reactions on the 18th green could not have been more contrasting. When Australia's Lucas Herbert missed a five-foot par putt on the last, there was a grimace from him and a groan from the galleries.

The bogey meant he had missed a golden chance to become the first man to shoot 61 at one of the sport's blue-riband events. Shortly afterwards, Sam Burns of the United States chipped in from a greenside bunker to also record an eight-under-par round of 62.

Golf.title: Padraig Harrington shot 80 at the Open. Then came an even bigger surprise
Golf.summary: Padraig Harrington wasn’t embarrassed by his first-round 80 at the Open, nor particularly impressed by his second-round 69. The post Padraig Harrington shot 80 at the Open. Then came an even bigger surprise appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — I’m staying near the course with some friends, one of whom has such a good grip it would give Lucas Glover grip envy. In other words, he knows golf. He said, speaking of Padraig Harrington’s first-round 80, “He must be so embarrassed.”

“I can almost guarantee you, he’s not,” I said. We were both doing the same math. Harrington won the Open, here at Royal Birkdale, in 2008, playing the final round in the final twosome with Greg Norman his own self. (Nick Faldo, doing TV commentary, looked at Norman’s yip-free putting stroke, at age 53, and said, “It’s not fair.”) Earlier this month, Harrington won the U.S. Open at Scioto, the senior one, for the 50-and-over crowd. Paddy is 54.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau takes subtle swipe at Nick Faldo as Jackson Suber sets Open pace
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau takes subtle swipe at Nick Faldo as Jackson Suber sets Open pace The Guardian
Golf.body:
From no clue and no strategy to no explanation. Who or what is eating Bryson DeChambeau? Maybe the coming days will reveal all. Then again … A fine and widely unexpected start to the 154th Open Championship was not sufficient to alter DeChambeau’s uncommunicative approach towards anybody who may not be inclined to tickle his tummy. Following a fifth major round in a row, DeChambeau declined the opportunity to speak to eagerly assembled media. One once so garrulous has lost his tongue.

There was plenty to ask. Nick Faldo, who knows a thing or two about the claiming of the Claret Jug, asserted before an Open ball was struck. “I’d say it to his face, DeChambeau has zero clue of strategy,” Faldo said. Ouch.

Golf.title: Open whisperer Tom Watson is back at another Open. We picked his brain
Golf.summary: Five-time Open winner Tom Watson is at Birkdale this week, soaking up the scene and dishing tales from Opens past. The post Open whisperer Tom Watson is back at another Open. We picked his brain appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — It would not be a ridiculous overstatement to say that Tom Watson changed my life. When I was a teenager, in the 1970s, falling into this game, Watson was one of golf’s rising stars and also one of the game’s high priests. Usually, you are one or the other, but he was both.

I became enthralled by links golf watching Watson win the 1975 British Open at Carnoustie on TV. Now this is ridiculous: Watson’s first Open — he had never played in one previously — was my first Open; I had never watched one before. Watson won his fifth and last Open here at Birkdale in 1983. He almost won it again in 1984, at the Old Course. He almost won it again in 2009 at Turnberry. He was 59 and lost in a playoff. I was in the press tent when he came in and said, “This ain’t no funeral.” What a gift — four words on my way to 2,100, and a sense of balance, too.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau’s strategy keeps him on the heels of surprise Open leader
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau’s strategy keeps him on the heels of surprise Open leader The Independent
Golf.body:
Unknown American Jackson Suber was the surprise leader of the Open at Royal Birkdale but it was compatriot Bryson DeChambeau making waves on and off the course. By the time the 26-year-old world number 115 had signed for a five-under 65, DeChambeau had left his mark on the links and six-time major winner Sir Nick Faldo with a sarcastic response to claims he had “zero clue on strategy”.

A fast and fiery Birkdale burned Masters champion Rory McIlroy who, as a late afternoon starter, got the more difficult wind and crusty greens and missed at least three putts from inside four feet in a round of 72 which left him seven off the lead.

Golf.title: Brown leads English contingent at The Open as McIlroy struggles
Golf.summary: When England's World Cup hopes were extinguished, it paved the way for the home golfers to take centre stage at the Birkdale Open - led by the colourful Dan Brown.
Golf.body:
English hopes for a first Open winner for 34 years were boosted with eight players under par after the first round - but Masters champion Rory McIlroy ended the day seven shots off the lead.

McIlroy endured a rollercoaster first round at Royal Birkdale which included six bogeys and four birdies in his two-over round of 72. American Jackson Suber leads the way on five under par, one shot ahead of England's Dan Brown and South Korea's Im Sung-jae, with Scotland's Robert MacIntyre also starting well and reaching three under.

Golf.title: Winners and Losers from Day 1 of the Open Championship
Golf.summary: From Bryson DeChambeau's 'strategy' to surprising struggles from major champs, here's who won — and lost — on Day 1 at Royal Birkdale. The post Winners and Losers from Day 1 of the Open Championship appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
They say you can’t win the Open Championship on Thursday, but you sure can win a spot in this column. Here’s an assortment of who won (and lost) at Royal Birkdale on Day 1. That would be Matthew Baldwin, who is from Southport, has been a member at Royal Birkdale for 23 years and hit the opening tee shot of Thursday’s first round. He shot a respectable two-over 72, but that moment will stand out:

“It was an incredible feeling. It was terrifying. It was overwhelming. But it’s something that will stay with me for the rest of my life.” That would be Matthew Fitzpatrick, who entered the week as red-hot World No. 3 and arguably the trendiest pick in the field but played a fairly blah opening round of two-over 72.

Golf.title: Bryson DeChambeau is golf's media superstar. He's not talking to the media
Golf.summary: Bryson DeChambeau refused to answer questions after firing one of the rounds of the day at the Open Championship, following a recent trend. The post Bryson DeChambeau is golf’s media superstar. He’s not talking to the media appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
SOUTHPORT, England — Human beings resist easy definitions. They resist blanket judgements. They require nuance and complexity and depth and texture. And in a sport filled with strange and vexing human beings, no player is better than Bryson DeChambeau at convincing us to believe the opposite.

Bryson’s life as a professional golfer has been like an entrapment scheme for critical thinkers — an endless ping-pong between “absolutely loved” and “completely hated” that has spanned at least six years, two professional tours, two major championship victories, a high-profile bullying story, a few thousand protein shakes and many, many million YouTube views. A scheme that continued with a new chapter on Thursday afternoon at the 154th Open Championship, when an R&A official informed reporters that DeChambeau would not be speaking to them despite shooting one of the rounds of the day at Royal Birkdale, continuing a major championship blackout from the golf press that dates back to a first-round 76 at the Masters on April 9 and has arrived with no apparent reason or explanation.

Golf.title: These comfy golf shoes have become the only ones I'll walk in | I Tried It
Golf.summary: The Skechers Blade Tour golf shoes have solidified themselves as my go-to golf trip shoe. The post These comfy golf shoes have become the only ones I’ll walk in | I Tried It appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
Welcome to I Tried It, a GOLF.com series about golf items — apparel, gear, accessories, etc. — that we’ve recently taken out for a spin. We’re here to give our honest, no-frills takes on the latest and greatest golf or golf-adjacent items. So, scroll down to read about what we love about golf’s newest (or new to us) products.

Over the last couple of years I’ve had the opportunity to work with the Softspikes team, and that relationship led into me becoming a big golf shoe nerd. First and foremost, spikes are an absolute must. I refuse to wear spikeless shoes, and I really don’t even recognize those offerings as being golf shoes. The one variable that never mattered too much to me, however, was walking. I’ve been told many times from spikeless users that the most common reason they use spikeless over spiked shoes is that they are more comfortable to walk in.

Golf.summary: The Open Championship’s happiest player? It’s maybe amateur Mateo Pulcini, who trolled the crowd at Royal Birkdale. The post Open Championship’s happiest player? Maybe the one … who trolled the crowd appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
By all accounts, he’s as considerate as they come, and no one seems more happy-go-lucky, though his golf would bring anyone joy. In January, in a playoff, he won the Latin America Amateur Championship, giving him tee times in April at the Masters, last month at the U.S. Open and this week at the Open Championship. At those first two majors, the 25-year-old amateur missed the cut, but he said he’s felt grateful, and this week has been just as welcome.

“It was everything what I was expecting and more,” Pulcini said. “The treatment is the one that stands out the [most], like how the people in the locker room, like the grill room, players lounge, everything, it’s been unbelievable. The organization of this tournament is unbelievable again.

Golf.title: He has 10 tattoos and smokes on the course. And he's 1 off the Open Championship lead
Golf.summary: Dan Brown isn't your typical Tour pro. But after a first-round 66 at the Open Championship he's chasing a Claret Jug. The post He has 10 tattoos and smokes on the course. And he’s 1 off the Open Championship lead appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
The 31-year-old English pro Dan Brown has a lumberjack’s beard, a nicotine addiction and “about” 10 tattoos, three of which, behind his ear, that depict “little birds,” Brown said Thursday from Royal Birkdale. Maybe Brown should add three more to his collection; that would bring his tally to the same number of birds he made in the opening round of the 154th Open Championship. That’s six, for those of you not counting along at home, which helped Brown to a four-under 66 that has him just one off the first-round lead — and surely prompting at least a few American golf fans to ask their favorite LLM about the 136th-ranked player in the world.

Brown, who has won twice on the DP World Tour but spent this season largely on the PGA Tour, is from Northallerton, about a two-and-a-half drive northeast of Birkdale. He dropped out of college after just a few months to pursue his golf dreams, and not only is he not related to the famous author with whom he shares a name but he also has read none of that Dan Brown’s works, or at least he hadn’t as of two years ago.

Golf.title: The biggest mistake golfers make after a swing change (and how to fix it)
Golf.summary: GOLF Teacher to Watch Chad Gibbs explains the biggest mistake he sees his players make after a big swing change. The post The biggest mistake golfers make after a swing change (and how to fix it) appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
We have all seen the cycle: a golfer begins making immediate progress with more solid contact, better sequencing and a more efficient swing. Then they hit one poor shot and become confused. They mistakenly believe that an improved swing should never produce a bad result. Like a dog chasing its tail, they quickly abandon the adjustment and return to the familiar, faulty habits that created their inconsistency in the first place.

As teaching pros, it is our job to pull students out of this “rabbit hole.” My approach to teaching golf has fundamentally evolved over the last several years. I used to focus almost exclusively on fixing the golf swing and improving ball flight. My primary objective was to repair the motion, which often left students believing their swing was broken. Although I recognized the negative impact of that mindset, I continued coaching through that same lens during every lesson.

Golf.title: He's a links-golf rookie. And he leads the Open Championship
Golf.summary: Jackson Suber, in his first trip to Europe and playing links golf, is off to a fantastic start at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. The post He’s a links-golf rookie. And he leads the Open Championship appeared first on Golf .
Golf.body:
This time of year, come Open Championship week, it’s trendy to pick gritty golfers. Or low-ball hitters or great wind players or guys who can move it both ways. It’s easy to like the Matt Fitzpatricks and Justin Roses and Tyrrell Hattons — the guys who grew up on this side of the Atlantic and are familiar with links golf.

But what about relatively unknown, links-golf rookies? Because one of them is leading the 154th Open Championship. Jackson Suber, the 26-year-old second-year PGA Tour player, played the back nine at Royal Birkdale in five-under 31 on Thursday to shoot 65 and steal the Round 1 clubhouse lead from Sungjae Im and Daniel Brown (66).

Badminton.title: China Open: Tide Turned
Badminton.summary: China Open: Tide Turned BWF World Tour
Badminton.body:
Title favourites Wang Zhi Yi and Chen Yu Fei turned the tables on familiar foes to book their VICTOR China Open 2026 quarterfinal places on Thursday. Two-time defending champion Wang ended a three-match losing streak against Korean Sim Yu Jin with an assured 21-16 21-15 victory, keeping alive her bid to become only the second player in tournament history to win three consecutive women’s singles titles after Jiang Yanjiao (2008-2010).

Having struggled to find answers in their previous meetings, Wang was pleased with the way she stayed composed when the pressure mounted. “Every match is a new one. You’ve just got to stay in the moment, focus on what’s in front and think about tomorrow when it comes,” said the world No.2.

Badminton.title: China Open: Outsiders Steal Show
Badminton.summary: China Open: Outsiders Steal Show BWF World Tour
Badminton.body:
Wednesday at VICTOR China Open 2026 served a reminder that rankings sometimes count for little, as a trio of inspired performances sent fancied second and seventh seeds crashing out in Changzhou.

The biggest statement came from Denmark’s Rasmus Gemke, who produced his best victory in years to stun men’s singles second seed Kunlavut Vitidsarn 21-13 8-21 21-19. The world No.30 held his nerve after the deciding game reached 19-all, sealing his first win over the Thai world No.2 in three years and his first victory against a top-five player since defeating then world No.4 Li Shi Feng at the China Masters in November 2023.

Badminton.title: China Open: Rescued by Resolve
Badminton.summary: China Open: Rescued by Resolve BWF World Tour
Badminton.body:
Three match points down and staring at another early exit, Weng Hong Yang found something that had been missing for much of 2026 – belief. The 2024 champion produced the comeback of the opening day, saving three match points at 20-17 before completing a thrilling 15-21 21-17 22-20 victory over men’s singles third seed Anders Antonsen in 84 unforgettable minutes at VICTOR China Open 2026.

It was a finish few inside the Olympic Sports Center Gymnasium saw coming. Weng had spent most of the afternoon chasing the Dane. After falling 11-6 behind in the opening game, he fought back to level at 14-all before Antonsen regained control. The Chinese player responded with a steadier display in the second game to force a decider but the momentum swung back heavily in Antonsen’s favour as he raced to a commanding 12-4 lead.
